utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, before we start, I think we have the list of the witnesses to discuss. This Trial Chamber has been seized of the Prosecution's supplemental filing concerning rebuttal case filed confidentially on the 3rd of October, 2002, whereby the Prosecution is informing the Chamber about the order of hearing of the rebuttal evidence. This Trial Chamber has already made a decision on the Prosecution's filing concerning rebuttal case issued on the 20th September 2002, in which the Chamber ordered the Witness ACD, in the current filing, to be heard in the course of the rebuttal. In this decision, this Trial Chamber has not granted the permission to hear the Witness B and E in the current filing, and we believe that the current filing may be considered as a motion to hear the new witnesses. Considering that the rebuttal hearing is scheduled today, and therefore, there's not sufficient time to await written response from the Defence, so this Trial Chamber would like to hear the response from the Defence counsel about those two new witnesses proposed by the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, good morning; good morning, Your Honours. What has been happening here lately doesn't make any sense and has nothing to do with the equality of arms. What was happening to us immediately before the beginning of these proceedings, before the 10th of September of last year, is now repeating. What the Prosecutor did by submitting to us at the last moment 17 binders that I haven't had the time to look at until this very day. We are watching the same film over and over again. The Prosecutor does not abide by your decision on the limitations of the evidence during those proceedings. He's introducing new evidence, new witnesses, without giving us the time to study the exhibits, their scope and their contents, and to be able to reply to them. When we were supposed to say something about the Defence witnesses during the rebuttal, we said that we did not see the need to hear these witnesses because we believe that the Trial Chamber is absolutely clear on our case. We could have called a number of witnesses, but we were prevented from doing so by the Prosecution. How? Simply, some of them they announced as their witnesses, but they haven't called them. The others they have contacted, thus preventing the Defence from calling them as their witnesses. The Prosecutor is thus planting a cuckoo's egg on us. He has delivered to us a statement by the investigator of the Prosecution team because it was to be expected that we couldn't take that for granted, that we would object to that statement, asking for its verification. We are claiming that the investigator's statement is not enough to prove the origin of the wooden rifle. She is supposed to provide hearsay evidence that she heard from a person whose name I'm not going to mention, and that person does not want to appear in front of this Trial Chamber. The Prosecutor is trying to stage a show, as if we were in a theatre. She is trying to create the illusion of truth by showing us, so to say, a wooden rifle that he was provided with by AID. And then, when the Prosecutor failed to transform illusion into the reality, then -- and he couldn't do that by means of Witness OO and Witness PP, then he calls the investigator rather than the person who allegedly held the wooden rifle in his hands. I suggest that the Trial Chamber denies the Prosecutor to do that. If the Trial Chamber accepts that as evidence, then we ask for a period of 15 days for us to prepare for the cross-examination and to verify the exhibits and to subject that wooden rifle to an expert opinion, because we have to be able to prove this forgery that was created by the Bosniak intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just briefly, I would like to address a new issue that is closely connected with what has been said so far. With regard to the Prosecutor's motion, we are now faced with the issue of the timing for the closing brief. According to the current schedule, the closing brief was scheduled for the 23rd of October, and the closing argument was supposed to take place on the 28th of October. As things stand currently, we believe that this scheduled is unsustainable, for the following reasons: Firstly, the schedule was drafted based on the expectations that the Prosecutor's rebuttal will adhere to the decision of the Trial Chamber. Now the Defence has been faced with new exhibits, new evidence, and thus we have wasted almost one week that we have allocated for drafting our closing brief. At the same time, by the decision of the 14th of October, we are expected to start our rejoinder, for which we now don't know how long it will last, whether we will be able to have this rifle, wooden rifle, for the expert opinion, and all that is preventing us from starting our closing brief and closing argument. Thirdly, something that is a very serious issue to my mind when it comes to the schedule, that is, the issue of the closing brief and when that should be delivered, and this has a lot to do with the equality of arms in these proceedings. It has been determined that both the Prosecution and the Defence should send the text of the closing brief to the Trial Chamber. However, the Defence is supposed to send that in the English, as well as the Prosecution. The Defence, when it has finally drafted the closing brief, will need at least seven days to have it translated into English. At the same time, the Prosecution doesn't need those seven days for the translation, because it will have already been drafted in English, and they will actually have seven days more. So because of this matter of translation, the two sides are not equal, because the Defence has less time to work on the closing brief. Bearing in mind all the situation, the Defence can say today that the 23rd of October, as the deadline for submitting the closing brief in English, is unacceptable because we have lost some time due to the new motion by the Prosecution. We need seven days for the translation, so we won't be in the position to deliver our closing brief by the 23rd of October. Therefore, we have the following proposal: To extend the deadline for the closing brief by seven days, which will allow us to have it translated, or, conversely, to order the Prosecution to translate their closing brief into Croatian and have it delivered to us within the deadline established by the Trial Chamber. We are calling upon the equality of arms in these proceedings, and we are calling upon the right of our client, who is entitled to have every piece of document in their mother tongue in order to be able to participate in these proceedings. So this is our proposal. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Your Honours, I don't know how to address you this morning, because what is happening here and what the Prosecutor is giving himself the right to do all the time, and what has he given the right himself to do finally, I really don't know how to call that. In any case, for seven days I have been thinking. On Saturday I arrived to find new faxes, new documents. I really cannot believe that what the Defence has been claiming all the while, and that is the Prosecution is not acting bona fide, that they still do that. Now we have been given exculpatory materials about the events in Jablanica and Konjic, although I'm sure, and I claim, that they had it a long time ago. However, we only received those documents three or four days ago. Not only that, Your Honours: While checking the materials that the Prosecution has sent us, I have come across some statements, the statements by the witnesses who have appeared before this Court, who have given their statements to the AID, and the Defence didn't have those statements when these witnesses appeared before the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution, on the other hand, must have had them at that time, because they have sent those statements to us within the Mostar file. This corroborates another fact, and that is that the Prosecutor knew very well that the proceedings took place not in Mostar, but in Konjic, under the so-called Sovic, the Sovici Indictment, and he obviously knew very well which documents he had, which he didn't have, but he manipulated with these documents. Now the Prosecutor may claim that they have 5.000 or millions of documents, 200 investigators. However, this corroborates the fact that they really have those documents. Now his argument will be: "I can't find all these documents. But whenever they are delivered to me, I will deliver them to the Defence." Your Honours, the story about the equality of arms before this Trial Chamber is simply ridiculous. The story about the equality of arms and the equality of possibilities given to the Prosecution and to the Defence is farcical. The Prosecution has so much power before this Trial Chamber and this Tribunal that only history and the future analysis will be able to show and demonstrate that, but it will be too late for some of the people who appear before this Tribunal. Your Honours, the Defence has been dramatically aggrieved. Can we please move into private session so I can give you some concrete examples?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have the witnesses waiting outside, and today we are going to hear the witnesses in the rebuttal proceedings. We will not discuss all those procedural matters at this stage. I believe that if you have some complaint to make, the best way is to file it in a written motion rather than discuss it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours, and this is how things happen, day in, day out, and I wonder here where justice is and what justice are we going to have if we are in a hurry because of the witnesses, as if the witnesses couldn't wait. Are we really not concerned with what is really going on? Can I really believe in justice? Why can't we have the witnesses wait for another two or three days? Are we going to lose? Is the justice going to lose if the witnesses wait? In any case, I will abide by your every ruling, but this is the end of our case and we are experiencing, at the hand of the Prosecution, what we are experiencing, and I think I have the right to tell you that. Let me go back to my original issue. To hear two investigators during the rebuttal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please do it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You've anticipated perfectly what is the issue of greatest concern to me at the moment, which is the fact that we have a nervous witness waiting outside, a victim of a lot of events which the Trial Chamber is not going to hear about during his testimony, but we've got a real nervous witness waiting outside, and despite my own interest in listening to the oratory of Mr. Krsnik and his ruminations about the meaning of justice, I think it would be more useful to us, and certainly more relevant to these proceedings, if we could deal with the witness who is waiting. It seems to me that most of the issues that are being raised by counsel this morning relate either to procedure or to a different rebuttal witness who has been approved. So I think much of what is being claimed, which is, if I may say, it's our view that counsel have taken great liberties with the realities of the situation this morning, we intend to address those specifically. But if I could just request the Trial Chamber to bear in mind that we do have a nervous witness whose testimony is not expected to take a very long time, and which I think after he's testified we could easily come back to these issues and take care of them in as much time as the Trial Chamber wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that Mr. Krsnik is going to tell about his reaction about the witness list at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. However, primarily I am surprised with the fact that my learned friend has interrupted me and that he has objected to something that the counsel, Defence counsel, had to say. I don't know whether that is the practice in the Anglo-saxon law. It is not the witness who is nervous, but the Prosecutor who is nervous. And as far as that is concerned, my client has been ill, sitting here for a year. Nobody has ever wondered about his situation, whether he's nervous, whether he is ill, what his situation is, and all of a sudden he expresses so much concern about his witness. Your Honours, Saturday we received the following message from the Prosecution, and that is that the witness who is now waiting nervously outside would be testifying about the Rados diary, and we received that on Saturday. But at the same time, your ruling was clear, and that is that he couldn't testify about that, but just about the circumstances indicated in your order, and that is the circumstances regarding Sovici and the participation of my client in any of these events. But we received this fax on Saturday, asking us whether we would object, half-witted as we are, he probably thought we wouldn't be able to read it and then he would be able to just do it during the direct examination. They should abide by your ruling. They shouldn't do it. However, they did it, and now we are afraid that things will be done as previously. I am not ready to cross-examine. I have to prepare myself. I'm not ready at all, and I'm not ready to cross-examine Mrs. Apolonia Bos. I hope she is not related to my learned friend sitting over there. And Mr. Prelec. These are new exhibits, new witnesses. What are they going to testify about? They had the time to testify during the proceedings, and those witnesses are going to give us secondhand evidence that they heard from a third hand. And if Mr. Prelec has already been heard by this Trial Chamber twice and now he has to come here so that the Prosecution could tender some new documents through him, but we have to be made aware of these documents in order to be able to reply to these documents, to be able to prepare. In that case, Your Honours, all the deadlines that you have given us can just not be adhered to. And finally, Your Honours, we have sent you a brief motion earlier this morning. We hope you will receive it by the end of the day. And when I asked you to move into private session, I wanted to talk about the witness that is waiting outside. But that is something I cannot say in open session. I must say that I'm not ready to cross-examine him, because I have come across another statement that is directly relative to him. I cannot say anything about that statement in the open session. What I'm trying to say is -- what I'm trying to ask you is for you, Your Honours, to warn our learned friends -- when you warn them that they should give us the exculpatory documents, they said that they didn't have them. Now all of a sudden they have them. Now I would like to ask them to give us all the exculpatory documents, and those are all the documents by the BH Army, the Court documents against AID that they have, because they have given them to our colleagues, Defence counsels in other cases. So we would like from them -- to receive from them all the exculpatory documents. This is their duty. They cannot manipulate with exculpatory documents. They are not here to carry out their own justice, but to serve justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. The microphone is on. I think it's best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to be clear that I understood the discussions on the Bench, or presume the discussions on the Bench were primarily ones about scheduling and the order in which to take these matters. Obviously the Prosecution wants very much to be heard on the substance of the allegations that have been made this morning before the Chamber would address any substantive ruling about that. We would be at a clear disadvantage if we're not given a chance to respond to rather serious unfounded allegations that have been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think there are three matters, you know, that we have to deal with at this moment. The first one is about the list of the witnesses. We understand that the Prosecution filed that motion for supplemental witnesses at a later stage. So at this moment, we are not quite sure whether we would like to hear the two other additional witnesses in the rebuttal proceedings for this week. So today we'll start with the Witness ACD in their current filings, and later on we'll make a decision whether there's any need to hear the two investigators in the OTP's team. Because all those rebuttal witnesses should be restricted first to the event related to Sovici and the Doljani, as well as the burial of Mr. Harmandzic. Second, to the identification of the wooden rifle; thirdly is to be restricted to the Rados diary. These three areas we'll decide at a later stage whether we are going to hear the two additional witnesses. As for the second issue, the postponement of the filing of the closing argument, we believe that this Trial Chamber give enough time to both parties to prepare their final closing argument compared with other Trial Chambers. So we would like to abide by the order we rendered previously in this respect. The third matter is about exculpatory materials alleged to be given recently by the Prosecution. This Trial Chamber knows next to nothing about this issue, and we are expecting the filings from both parties. It is so decided. Let's hear the first witness, please. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, may it please the Trial Chamber. Your ruling is just settled a couple of matters, but this first witness, we still have the issue and the problem that the Prosecutor just last Saturday faxed us information that he intends to elicit evidence from this first witness that is not in your prior ruling, in your prior order, and you've not addressed that issue yet, and that's the issue about this alleged Rados diary. They told us that two days ago. This first witness was restricted to Sovici, 17th and 18th of April. Now they intend to lead evidence about the Rados diary, we they claim they just found out about on Friday. That issue has not been resolved, unless it has, correct me, but if they're restricted to what your prior order was, I'm satisfied with that, and we'll make the objections as the witness testifies if they want to get into that additional area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we know next to nothing about this matter. Would you please give us some explanations about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's my problem. The Defence has now gone on for half an hour, without any response by the Prosecution, and that's our concern. We're not going to handle all these issues now, because of what the Chamber has already said. We're more than happy to address every issue and according to the Court's schedule we will.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me say first of all, as to the matter with the witness about to be called and the Rados diary. The witness was first seen by members of my staff on Friday. In the course of the day, completely -- it became clear for the first time that the witness had something to say about the Rados diary. It had never showed up in any prior interviews. It had simply never come up before. When it came to our attention, we respectfully submit, Your Honours, we did the only thing professionally appropriate to do, and we faxed that information to the Defence so that it indeed would not be heard for the first time, it would not be sprung on them during the witness's in-court testimony. So it's our position, whatever the Court's ultimate ruling would be, and of course we would abide by that, but the Chamber should please understand that we believe we have acted honourably and we have acted as soon as the information came to our attention. It is information which is indeed directly related to one of the rebuttal issues which the Chamber has said is proper for the Prosecution to tender evidence on. It is not a new issue. It is the Rados diary issue. And we respectfully submit, Your Honour, on that matter, that we have done everything possible to give notice and we have conducted ourselves quite fairly and honestly in the matter. I won't belabour it on this point, Your Honour, save this: When I compare the allegations and assertions that is have been made by counsel this morning to the numerous problems and lack of disclosure that the Prosecution received over the past four or five months in the Defence case, it pales in comparison. It pales in comparison. This Prosecution team has conducted itself honourably throughout these proceedings. We respectfully submit. I'm happy to respond to any specific allegation. I'm confident that I will be able to show the Chamber that the allegations made are baseless. I feel also compelled, Your Honour, to say that, in terms of the schedule this Court has given just now, the indication of, I don't think it would be appropriate for me to -- for us to go forward with some misunderstanding. The Witness C on our list of supplemental filing has refused to appear. He will not come to The Hague. He will not appear. Witness D is not available to testify until tomorrow. So the only witness, apart from Witnesses B and E, the only witnesses we would be able to call today the witness list that is number A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your information. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Mr. President, with regard to the decision that you rendered today about time limits for submitting the closing brief. I would now like to make a verbal request, pursuant to Rule 21 -- Article 21 of the Statute, paragraph 4. I would request that the closing brief of the Prosecutor be provided to our client in his mother tongue, and that he respect the same time limit that we have to respect when providing the Prosecution with the brief in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. The Rules do not require that, plainly. Pleadings don't have to be translated into the B/C/S language. That's clear Tribunal jurisprudence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have spent enough time on those issues. We could deal with it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations with my colleagues, we are going to hear the witness about his testimony on the events related to Sovici and Doljani, as well as the burial of Harmandzic. We're also going to hear the witness's testimony about the Rados diary, because this matter was one of the three matters granted by this Trial Chamber. Of course, we believe that the Defence counsel will be in a disadvantaged position at this moment, so we decided that the Defence counsel could conduct its cross-examination tomorrow. It is so decided. Could we have the witness, please. Are there any protective measures for this witness? Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is requesting pseudonym and facial distortion. I believe he will be Witness AF, as in Frank, Alpha Francis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections for the protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't hear what my colleague said. I was consulting with my colleague. I have no objections to make to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Seric, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The request has been granted. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I inquire at what time the Trial Chamber intends to take the first break this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stringer:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we begin with your testimony, I will inform you that the Trial Chamber has granted the request that you made for protective measures, so that when you testify, we're going to refer to you by a pseudonym, which is "Witness AF." So I'll ask you in your testimony not to mention your own name or the names of family members, persons, in a way that you would identify you. Okay? Let me also mention: I think that it's important that all of us can hear you, and so if you could just try to remember to keep your voice up, it would assist those who are doing the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move the microphones a little closer to the witness, please, also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the usher is showing you a piece of paper, and I want to ask you if you can look at the paper, tell us whether your name and your birth date appear correctly on the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we go into private session for just a few preliminary questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, also just one general question. Sir, are you of the Bosnian Muslim faith or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as someone who lived in Sovici, did you live in the area of the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, first I want to take you back a few months from April and to the late part of 1992 or the early part of 1993, and I want to ask you whether during that time you became associated in any way with the HVO, or particularly, the 3rd Mijat Tomic Battalion of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how that came about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, they were making a road, Sovici-Jablanica, that route, and they suggested there was heavy equipment there on parts of the road, and they needed to get -- designate four men to guard the machines, two Muslims and two Croats. So I and another person, who was also a Muslim, were designated and two colleagues were designated to represented the Croats. And they did this job. And I was on the list with their soldiers all the time. I was on the list of their soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were on the list of their soldiers, which group are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Mijat Tomic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have that task in April of 1993, that is, to guard the road-making machines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, to the very end, to the time when the village of Sovici was attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if perhaps my colleagues will allow me just to ask a couple more directive questions. Witness, did you -- your task, then, too was to guard or to watch over this machinery during the night-time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform or did you have any weapons that were issued to you by the 3rd Mijat Tomic Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We didn't have any weapons, but we did have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you then go, on the night of the 16th of April, 1993, to go fulfil this task and to watch over the road-making machinery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time of day did you finish with that task and return home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: In the morning, about half past 5.00, half past 6.00, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now this would be the morning of the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already referred to an attack, I believe. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what happened in Sovici on that day? What happened to you and other members of your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Something surprising happened after all of that. About 7.30/quarter to 8.00, the shelling of the village started. No one knew what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from what location the shelling was coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: From the Risovac area, from Sovici Vrata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I was on the road leading from the house to the workshop, as there was no electricity. I went to the car to listen to the news, and halfway down the road I heard intense shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why there was no electricity on that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The electricity supply had been cut off two days ago, because Jablanica had been shelled two days earlier on, from the direction of Risovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the shelling started then, did you remain in your house with other members of your family then for that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No. As I had a young baby and my brother's young baby in the house, who had been born 15 days prior to the attack, I took the baby to my uncle's house, where there was a concrete slab.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also live in the village of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made reference to a concrete slab. Perhaps you could give us more information about that. Was his house different than yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. Our houses had been constructed out of wood for the most part. It was a wooden construction. The roof was wooden, so it was very easy for a shell to pass through and hit the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your uncle's house different in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: What do you mean? In what respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was his house constructed in a way that made it stronger to withstand the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was a newly constructed house. It had been constructed out of concrete and by using concrete slabs. It had two such slabs. It had been perhaps one year earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain with the others at your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We spent the whole day there, until about 4.00 or 5.00, sometime in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the shelling last that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, it lasted for the entire day, from morning to night, until late at night, until 8.00 and after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you remained there until about 4.00 or 5.00 in the late afternoon or evening. Then what happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. Two soldiers appeared from up above, from the direction of Risovac. They had visited us on previous occasions. They would come to eat something. They came and they asked us -- they said if anyone has weapons, that they should be taken to Stipe Pole's house. They said that nobody should be touched, that it was a matter of policy. There were negotiations of some kind, so that nothing should happen to anyone. He said that we were safe, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of -- or which unit or organisation these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: These soldiers belonged to a unit from Posusje. They were from Posusje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in the HVO or the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they said that the weapons should be taken to someone's house. I wanted to make sure we have it correct in the record. What was the name of the person where the -- whose house was it that the weapons should be taken to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The house belonged to Stipe Pole, further down below, in Srednja Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then did you begin moving down towards Srednja Mahala and the house of Stipe Pole?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I object to the leading nature of the questions. That's a leading question, and we're beyond background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, you know this is rebuttal proceedings. During the rebuttal proceedings, you know, we have to lead this witness directly to the events that he's going to testify. So in the rebuttal proceedings, to a great extent we'll allow the leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The leading questions are allowed in the rebuttal case and the rejoinder case; is that the Rules?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We don't have to spend much more time on the background issues. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers, were they armed, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They told you to surrender your weapons at Stipe Pole's house, you said. So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Those who had weapons took them down there, and then they locked them in Stipe Pole's basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go down there from your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did other members of your family go with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. All the male members, both those who were of age, as well as adults, went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go by yourself or were you accompanied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The two soldiers went with us. We went all of us together. The whole group of us who were in the house at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at this point, did you hear or learn anything about what was taking place in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything specific, but it all sounded like a game, like something funny, like a child's game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the local commander of the ABiH in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Dzemal Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he was doing at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: He was the one informing the population of the village, asking them to surrender their weapons, promising that nothing would happen to any of us, that he personally negotiated with Tuta, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of Tuta before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, but I never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you have any weapons that you surrendered on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We had weapons in the house, weapons that we had from 1967 on. Those were hunters' rifles, two hunters' rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you get those rifles? I say on the day, the 17th, where were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: They were in the house, and nobody wore them. Those rifles belonged to my father. He had them for 20 years, used them when he went hunting. He used them for sports. So nobody wore those rifles at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the rifles in your uncle's house or in your own house on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: In our own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use those rifles at all on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Stipe Pole's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We surrendered the weapons, and then they locked us in the basement of that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day was it, approximately, when you arrived at Stipe Pole's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: It was around 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the usher's assistance, I'd like to show the witness a photograph, one that's been marked P6.8. I've got one in my hand that we can work with, if it makes things easier. Yes, on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could look at the photograph that's to your side there. I want to ask you if you see the house of Stipe Pole anywhere in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take the red marker, please, and put a circle around that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have also Exhibit P6.7 that you can ... we'll get to that one in a minute. Witness, how long did you remain in the basement at the house of Stipe Pole that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Until 9.00, or maybe even longer, in the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many others were held in the basement that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: There were over 70 people locked in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these other people had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: All of them were from the village, from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they belong to any particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No. They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at about 9.00, or at some point, did you leave the basement of Stipe Pole's house and go to a different location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. Around 9.00, the local leaders came, the local leaders of the HVO. They lined us up and then they took us to the Sovici school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the Sovici school on the other photograph, P6.7?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then turning to the photograph at your side, can I ask you to place a circle around the Sovici circle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what is the approximate distance from the house of Stipe Pole to the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Two hundred or two hundred and fifty metres, as the crow flies, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you and the others remain in the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We spent the night there, and we stayed there the whole next day until sometime in the afternoon, late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened during that night, that first night that was spent in the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Some soldiers came. People were harassed, taken out, taken back, interrogated, and that went on until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you recognised a couple of these soldiers who came from Posusje. Do you know what other HVO units were present, if any, in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: There were a lot of units that I had never seen before. There were a lot of Tuta's men, and other local men. There were a lot of men from Posusje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Tuta's men. What was it about them that allowed you to identify them as Tuta's men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: They had the insignia and their uniforms were different. They were not the same as the uniforms of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten or mistreated or interrogated during that night at the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, then, what happened the following morning, which I believe would be the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: On the following morning, Mr. Tuta came with his escorts and our local leaders also came, and they freed a room in the school. They gave it to Mr. Tuta. And all day long he interrogated and mistreated the detained soldiers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who accompanied him? You mentioned some other persons. Do you know their names or their positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I don't know their positions, but they mentioned the name Cikota, Robi and some other names. I had never seen them before, but in any case, there were a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this Tuta in uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of vehicle he arrived in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: It was a white jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did he remain in the Sovici school on that day? I'm talking about Tuta.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. He remained there some time, but not all day. He disappeared at one point. And then he -- the local commanders came later on. Tuta also came again. They lined us up in front of the school building, and one of our local commanders, Ivan Rogic, produced a piece of paper from his pocket and started reading, saying that we were sentenced because of the rebellion against the legal government of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you interrogated on that day by Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Not me personally, but others, yes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in the school building itself for the entire day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Not me personally, but others did. I was taken away by his soldiers. I was mistreated all day long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did his soldiers take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: They took me to the summer kitchen belonging to Ivan Pole and they intended to chop my head off with an axe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could come back to the last photograph that I showed the witness. I think it was 7.6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I could ask you again to look at this photograph. Do you see the place that you've described as the smoke house on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take the green marker and put a circle around this smoke house, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the reason -- were you informed the reason why you were taken to this smoke house and why they threatened to decapitate you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I know. Somebody maliciously said that I had a sniper, that I hadn't surrendered, and they wanted to force me to surrender it, although I never had it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No. No. I surrendered my rifle, but optical instruments they thought I had, and I never had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this incident in the smoke house, were you returned back to the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No. I was returned behind the school, where I found some people who were tied and who were prostrated on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Then my hands were also tied. They ordered me to lie down next to them. There was a man standing above us with his rifle aimed at us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, then what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: A neighbour came by. His name is Ivan Kolak. He came from his barn. He asked us what was going on, and I told him, "I cannot seem to persuade these people that I don't have the sniper's scope. I never had it. But I can't seem to persuade them that that is true."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Kolak say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Mr. Kolak said, "Guys, I know the man. He really doesn't have it. We used to hunt together. We used to hang out together. But you can do whatever you want to do."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then did the soldiers allow you to join the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered me to stand up, that I -- they untied my hands and then they ordered me to untie the others who were tied up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that point, then, near the school, where did you go and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: They returned us to the area in front of the building. There were some people lined up there already. All around the school there was the army guarding us so that nobody would escape. Then they lined us up in front of Stipe Pole's house, on the plateau, and that's where we were forced to load buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a few minutes ago you mentioned a speech that was made, and I wanted to ask you just a few questions about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: When we returned to the area behind the school, we found some people lined up there. We joined that line. And then Ivan Rogic took a piece of paper from his pocket, started reading, mentioning some rebellion, that we were the ones who rebelled against somebody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Ivan Rogic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Ivan Rogic was somebody who lived there. He was a neighbour of ours, and he used to work in Jablanica as a judge, in the municipal court there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other HVO people were present when he was giving this speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was there. Mr. Tuta and others were there. There were a lot of soldiers, quite a few of the local commanders, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this speech was finished what occurred next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Then they drove us to the plateau in front of Stipe Pole's house, where a bus had already been waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and the others then board the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We were taken towards Doljani, in the direction of Doljani, and then we took another road, and they returned us towards the Sovici-Vrata, the Sovici gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the final destination that you eventually reached?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The final destination was when we arrived in Ljubuski. That was in the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you and the others treated during the bus ride to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Terrible. Really, really badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the prisoners who received particularly bad treatment during that bus ride?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Dzemal suffered most, and others, all those who were in the front of the bus, closer to the driver, they suffered the most beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was Dzemal who? What was the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any soldiers who were particularly brutal to the prisoners during this bus ride?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I do. Robi accompanied us, and Cikota was there all the time, all the way to Ljubuski. And there were some other soldiers there as well. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 15930 to 15933.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness. Now, you arrived in Ljubuski, as you said, the following morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we're going to -- we're just about at the point of taking our morning break, and we're going to move through your -- we're going to move past your experience at Ljubuski. I'm not going to ask you about that, but simply to ask you how long you remained as a prisoner in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's beyond the scope of this witness's -- it's beyond the scope of this Trial Chamber's order as to what this witness could testify to. So the bus ride, as a matter of fact, and I ask that that be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment we don't know whether this question is related to the subject-matter of the rebuttal proceedings. Mr. Stringer, would you please enlighten us on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think I just said that I'm not going to ask the witness about anything that happened in Ljubuski. We could spend a good full hour on that. But I think it's necessary to at least establish the period of time that the witness was held in Ljubuski so that then it makes sense to the Trial Chamber when we discuss his arrival date at the Heliodrom, which does take us directly into the next part of his testimony. So I think that counsel is being a bit overly technical here. I'm just simply trying to place this in a context so the Trial Chamber can know what is the sequence of events, without going into the specific details or evidence about what happened in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honours, we filed a written submission two weeks ago where we alleged that the Prosecution was doing nothing more than bolstering and shoring up the weaknesses in their case. You denied that, and here we are. It's an improper question. It goes beyond the scope of what this Trial Chamber said this witness could testify concerning, and it seems that the Trial Chamber's orders get rewritten continuously by the Prosecution in the manner in which they ask the questions, in the manner in which they get by with what they do. We object. You make the call, Your Honours, but it is absolutely beyond it. He can testify -- when he -- got to the Heliodrom, perhaps, but we object, Your Honours, strongly about anything about Ljubuski, the bus ride. This shouldn't have been testified to. I ask that that be stricken. And the next subject that he has to testify is only about the burial, the alleged burial, of Harmandzic, not about the Heliodrom, not about Ljubuski or anything else, Your Honours. And we object. You entered an order. We think the Prosecution should abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can't be any more clear, Mr. President. I'm not going to ask him about Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand that. I think you informed us that you are going to establish the sequence of the events step by step, Mr. Stringer. I think this question is allowed in that aspect. But I hope you could come to that subject-matter as soon as possible so is that we don't have to spend much more time to establish the background issue and the sequence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can do it in one question before the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you spend approximately a month and a half as a prisoner in Ljubuski before being transferred to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're ready for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, I want to take you to the time that you spent at the Heliodrom, and specifically in respect of one event that occurred during the time that you were detained there. First of all, just so the Trial Chamber knows: You've testified that you spent about a month and a half in Ljubuski before going to the Heliodrom. How long did you remain as a detainee in the Heliodrom before you were eventually released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, we spent a total of 11 months in the camp, so about 9 1/2 months in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I'm going to ask you about an incident. First let me ask you this: During the time that you were a prisoner at the Heliodrom, were you involved in the burial of bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times were you involved in burying bodies, where were those bodies buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: On two occasions. The first time I was involved was at the so-called Muslim cemetery, in Miljkovici, where we buried 72 or 73 inmates; and on the second occasion, it was in the Liska Park cemetery. I buried someone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- the second occasion that you just mentioned, can you say again the name of the cemetery where that burial occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The first place was in Miljkovici, and on the second occasion we buried someone in Liska Park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the burial at Liska Park. First of all, do you recall approximately the month or the time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Not the exact date. I can't remember it. But it was in the summer. It was in July or in August, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, then, about that day, that incident, how it came to pass that you were involved in burying this particular body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, the first time I buried a body in Liska Park, it was a man who had been killed across the road from the medical centre. He had been killed in the street. Two inmates brought him to us, and we had been selected, three of us had been selected to dig a grave for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the beginning of that day just so that we get the full story. Where were you on that day? Where were you? Were you in the Heliodrom when that day began?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No. We were working near the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the day start? How did you get to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, every morning someone -- a driver came to fetch us. He was a soldier, a policeman. His name was Luka Stojanovski. He would come every morning and take a group of 30 to 40 people away to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he take you on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: On that day he took us to the command, to Mr. Stela. Two soldiers came to fetch us, the group of prisoners, and they took us to work in the medical centre area, down around Kontarevac, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever met Mr. Stela before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen him before this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever gone to work in this area before, the area that you described, the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. We went there quite often, almost every day for a two, three-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the usher's assistance I'd like to show the Witness Exhibit 14.4, which is a photograph. And for the record, this will be 14.4/5. And Mr. President, I should inform you that the previous two photographs that were used before the break are now marked as 6.7/3 and 6.8/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you could take a look at that photograph and tell me whether you recognise any of the areas that you've described in this testimony about this particular day in August or July. You mentioned a medical centre. Do you see that place in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's put the photograph on the ELMO. And then, Witness, if I could just ask you to take the pointer that's in front of you, and I'm going to ask you to first point out, if you can, the location of the medical centre that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The medical centre was here, this complex. These buildings here between the cross roads and the Bulevar, between the crossroad that leads from the roundabout up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could ask the usher just if we could move the photograph down in the direction toward the bottom so that we -- I'm sorry. The opposite way. We want to see more of the top half of the photograph. Yes. If we could just keep moving a little bit. That's good. That's good. Okay. Witness, do you recall what time of day you arrived in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We arrived there about 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. I can't remember the exact time, but it was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners arrived at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: There were about 40 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to the specific location, if you see it, where you arrived and where you were first received at that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, we arrived here and then went to this part, and from this location we were sent to work in these schools. We would dig trenches in the direction of the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you working in those areas that you've just pointed to, digging trenches and whatnot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, we worked for about two to three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we be more precise? Either the witness should mark this or write down the zone which he indicated in a hesitant way with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Stringer, would you please give some specific directions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For the record, I can't agree that there was any hesitation, but I think that's obviously for the Trial Chamber to consider.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, taking perhaps the red marker, can you just perhaps draw a line that would indicate the location of the trench or the trenches that you were working on on this particular day after you arrived in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes. I'll mark it on the entire photograph. I'll mark the directions of our movement, if that isn't going to bother you. We went in this direction, then we followed this route. We passed through these two houses and continued down here, passed behind these buildings, and then we passed through the building here, up until this point, and then we have this part here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving from that work that you were performing on that day, I want to bring you now to the burial of the body that you've mentioned. Where were you when you first were tasked with burying a body or being involved in the burial of a body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The first time we buried a body, that was on the road by the medical centre. We buried this body in Liska Park. And the other bodies, we buried them after the action that took place on the 17th of September, in the morning of the 18th, in the Miljkovici cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to bring you back again to the Liska Park, and if you could just tell us the story about that, from the very beginning. Where were you when you first became involved in the burial of this body? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: We were in front of the medical centre. We were carrying sandbags, sealing the windows, and breaking through certain walls to make it possible to pass from one room to another. This is the work we did all the time, and whenever it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of you at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, when we were taken to work, they would line us up in front of the command, where Mr. Stela was, and then usually two soldiers would appear to take us down to the line. And down at the line there was someone called Ernest. He was mostly there. He was the person who was in charge of us and of everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings that day with Ernest in connection with the burial of the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, but first of all he lined all of us up, and then he asked, "Is there anyone who is strong?" No one responded. No one came forward. He then selected a man and asked him whether he could carry 50 kilos. He said, "I don't know, sir." He then ordered him to pick him up, to try to carry him, and in fact this is what he did, and Ernest then told him, "You see, you can carry 50 kilos. Why didn't you respond?" He remained silent. Then he selected another person and took him with him behind the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened -- where were you -- or where were you placed after they went away behind the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: He returned again and shut the rest of us up in a garage next to a house. That's where he shut us up, and he placed a soldier by the door to make sure that no one came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say that he put you into this garage, who is it who did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Ernest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you were in the garage, did he return then after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: He returned, Ernest returned, and took three of us out. He took us behind that garage. He took us to a garden. He gave us shovels too. And there he said that we should dig a grave there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: That we should dig a hole for the garbage there. Correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there again Witness. Taking the marker, if you're able to identify this spot on the photograph, can you place a number 1 on the location where you were instructed to dig this hole for the garbage.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: That was somewhere here, in the garden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you place a number 1 there? Witness, could I ask you to put a number 1 on that location? I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So then after you were instructed to dig this hole, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, we were ordered to finish this in 15 minutes' time, which we did. After some time had passed, these two inmates turned up and they brought a corpse that we were to bury there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which two inmates, now, just so that we're clear? Which two inmates are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I'm referring to the two men who had previously been taken away by Ernest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when they -- you say they brought a corpse. Do you know how they -- how did they actually carry or bring the corpse to your location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, they were holding the corpse by the arms and by the legs, because there were only two of them, and the man was big; he weighed a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they using anything else to carry the body, or was it -- were they just simply carrying the body by itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was some kind of a carpet, part of a carpet, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where they got this material that they were using to carry the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I don't know. Ernest must have given it to them when they took that blanket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We've gotten a couple of different words for this item. Can you describe the thing that they were using to carry the body? Can you describe that thing in greater detail, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, it was some kind of a blanket. It wasn't really very big. There was perhaps half of a blanket. And they put the man on this blanket, but they were pulling him rather than carrying him, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen a blanket like this previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, there were a lot of blankets of that kind in the trenches, in the dugouts that were used by the soldiers. They used them to cover the trenches. And when it was cold, they would cover themselves with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the source of those blankets, where they were manufactured or who provided them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could see, these blankets were mostly delivered by humanitarian organisations. They would distribute these blankets to refugees, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, if you can, the colour of the blanket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It wasn't entirely blue and it wasn't entirely black either; it was something in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the other two prisoners had retrieved this body? Where had the body been before they brought it to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I really didn't carry the body until they brought the body to us, to that hole. They said that they had found the body in the street, near the medical centre, and that Ernest had ordered them to take it down to the crossroads of the Bulevar and then to take it back to where it was. And then they took it to the hole where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen the body before, prior to that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: No, I hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at photograph -- the photograph there that's next to you, 14.4, are you able to point to the locations where the body had been retrieved before it was brought to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: I really didn't carry the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although you said that you would allow suggestions, this is really ridiculous, because the witness has just said that he hadn't seen where the witness was before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me clarify it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you learn from the other two prisoners where they had gone to retrieve the body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They said that they had retrieved it from a spot across the road from the medical centre. He was -- the body was in the street, and Ernest ordered them to take it down to crossroads, to the Bulevar. This is what they did, and they returned the body again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they have to take it down to the crossroads before bringing it back to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is attempting something that isn't allowed again. He is asking the witness to speculate about what other people were thinking and about what they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, because, you know, the Prosecutor asked the question. Did you learn from the other prisoners where they had gone to retrieve the body? This is somehow hearsay evidence. I agree with you in this aspect, but in the proceedings the hearsay evidence is allowed. The question is how much weight we put on those pieces of evidence. Mr. Stringer, you may continue, and bear in mind that it is not the first-hand evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- Witness, did you learn from the others, from the other two prisoners, the reason why they had to move the body or carry it down toward the Bulevar before moving it back toward your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, in fact they took the body down there because the BH Army was across the road, and this was supposedly to show them that a man had been killed and that we were then going back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn on that day, or subsequently, the reason why this body was being removed from this area in front of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Well, after all of this, when we had finished with the digging, a soldier appeared, who didn't allow the body to be buried there. He said that it would be an obstacle to people passing through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my question was a bit different. Did you learn on that day, or did you learn later, the reason why the body was removed from the confrontation area? Why was it removed versus just allowing it to stay there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: Actually, we didn't know why it was being removed, but after a certain period of time, Mr. Stela came and ordered Ernest to clean everything, and I thought that he was implying that garbage or rubbish be cleaned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back, then, to the arrival of the body at this location where you had dug the hole, or the grave: What was the condition of the body generally when they brought it to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: The body was very badly damaged in the area of the head and in the area of the chest and in the area of the stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the body been -- had this person recently died, or are you able to give some indication whether this had been a dead person for a matter of minutes, hours, days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness is not a doctor, as far as I understand, and I don't think he is able to estimate the time when the person died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course this witness is not a doctor, but the Prosecutor was not going to ask about medical opinions. He just asked the impression, because this witness saw that body himself. You may proceed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer my last question? Just a general idea: Is this someone who had just died or had this person been dead for longer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: It seemed to me that the body had been dead for a while. There was a terrible stench around it. You couldn't be around the body for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned already -- maybe I should just ask you again. Can you give us a general idea the size or the dimensions of this body, and also the sex of this person, if it's not already clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AF
utterances.text: It was the body of a big man, a heavy man, who weighed over a hundred kilos. It was a well-developed man.
